content_type: Video transcript (Claude Code tutorial + Claude Co-work tutorial)
portion_doctrine: This portion contains comprehensive Claude Code + Claude Co-work operating manuals extracted from video transcripts. Segments 11-16 span Chapters 16-36 covering project management, deployment, context management, token optimization, skills creation, agent teams, git workflows, API deployment with Modal, and Claude Co-work setup. Material is highly technical with actionable patterns but heavily interspersed with video commentary, UI descriptions, and metaphors.
gold_summary: Operational framework for autonomous AI workflows: context compression, token budgeting, parallel agent orchestration, persistent memory systems (projects/skills/scheduled tasks), and distribution/monetization patterns. Primary value is in mechanics (not philosophy): how to structure systems for reuse, how to manage context windows, how to leverage parallelization for speed-time-token tradeoffs.
operating_rules: Context window = total tokens model can process at once (e.g., Opus 4.6 = 200k, Sonnet = 1-2M). Token budget is your operational ceiling.
Auto-compact buffer: when context hits ~33k tokens remaining (or ~99% full), Claude automatically compresses conversation history to free space. Manual /compact available.
System tools overhead: ~16,800 tokens consumed by default Claude Code tools (bash, web-fetch, grep, edit, write, etc.) before user sends first message. This is unavoidable and billed.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) tools are user-defined extensions. Each MCP server adds overhead (can be 5-20% of context depending on tool complexity). Use sparingly; tool descriptions exceeding 10% of context window trigger automatic tool search mode (load-on-demand).
Memory/MEMORY.md auto-loaded every session, consuming tokens. Minimize to 2-5k tokens max. Cloud.md system prompts (global + local) = ~10k tokens baseline.

Message ratio: only ~2.6-3% of context typically consumed by user messages/conversation. Majority consumed by system infrastructure (tools, MCP, memory). Optimize via high-information-density requests, not message count.
Agent teams cost 7x more tokens than standard sessions (each agent maintains own context window). Parallelization trades cost for speed; $1.3M tokens = hours of human time saved.

Git workflows (branches/worktrees): isolate parallel work, prevent file conflicts. Multiple agents on separate branches merge without stepping on toes. Merge conflicts require mediation; worktrees eliminate this risk.

Skills = reusable instruction files (Markdown + optional scripts). Load on-demand, don't consume context until invoked. Projects = persistent workspace (skills + context + memory baked in). One project per recurring workflow.
Scheduled tasks run on host machine when desktop app open; no APIs/third-party tools needed. Test manually first, then schedule at specified cadence (daily/weekly/monthly).
Modal (or similar serverless platform) enables free/cheap API endpoint deployment. $5-30 credits cover months of light usage. Skills can be wrapped as public URLs via webhooks.

Token management tier 1 (must-do): use /cost to monitor, /compact to compress, /context to audit usage. Tier 2 (should-do): RAG (retrieval-augmented generation), high-info-density prompts, reduced MCP overhead. Tier 3 (advanced): extended thinking mode, smaller models for sub-agents, custom compaction instructions.
named_methods: Plan Mode: Plan-first execution reduces token waste on research/loops. Front-load research, then build. Heavily used in proposal generator and agent teams workflows.
Context Compaction: Progressive summarization of conversation history, collapsing messages into high-density summaries. Auto-triggered at ~99% context usage.

Agent Teams Framework: Spawn N parallel agents on separate tasks/branches, then merge results. Debate agents (adversarial review) improve quality (validated by generative adversarial networks precedent). Requires orchestration to prevent file conflicts.
Git Worktrees: Multiple isolated working directories sharing Git history. Each agent/branch works independently, then merges to main. Eliminates cross-agent file stepping.

Proposal Generator Pattern: Voice transcript + prompt + Claude Code = landing page + proposal delivery. Time-to-output: 15-20 min end-to-end (including manual steps). Cost: ~free after Netlify setup (deployment cost = free tier).
Skills-to-URL Pipeline: Skill definition (Markdown checklist) + Modal API wrapper = public webhook. 2 minutes setup. Enables form-based skill invocation.

Co-Work Projects Pattern: Persistent folder + context MD files (about-me, brand-voice, working-preferences) + instructions auto-loaded every session. Memory compounds; no re-explaining needed after session 1.
Scheduled Task Automation: Write prompt once, pick cadence (daily/weekly/monthly), let Claude execute on schedule. Dispatch (SMS/text interface) allows mobile task submission to desktop runner.
Token Optimization via Sub-Agents: Use cheaper model (Sonnet) for sub-agents that do heavy lifting, Opus for orchestration. Smaller context = lower cost = faster iteration.

content_ideas: Build a 'Skills Library' template: reusable skill definitions (Markdown format) for common workflows (invoice processing, meeting notes, email drafting, social media scheduling). Open-source repo.
Create a 'Token Budget Calculator': given task scope (e.g., '1000 invoices', 'agent teams with 10 agents'), estimate token cost + actual cost in dollars. Helps operators plan spend.
Document 'Agent Team Patterns': security audits, website design iteration, code review/debate, content brainstorming. Each pattern with team composition, cost, expected time.
Build 'Project Starter Pack': folder structure + example about-me.md, brand-voice.md, working-preferences.md for different roles (marketer, developer, content creator, founder). Pre-filled.
Create 'Scheduled Task Cookbook': 30-40 common automation patterns (morning briefing, content research, email batch reply, invoice weekly summary, social media scheduler). Copy-paste ready.
Document 'MCP Server Audit': which servers are worth the token overhead, which aren't. Token cost vs. capability tradeoff chart.
Build 'Co-Work Setup Video': recorded walkthrough of folder structure + MD files + connector setup + first 3 projects. Template-heavy, ~15 min.
Create 'Skills Evaluation Rubric': how to judge if a skill is working (accuracy, consistency, time saved). Metrics to track output quality over time.
Document 'Token Optimization Playbook': step-by-step audit (run /context, identify top consumers, apply compression techniques). Reduce token usage by 30-50%.
Build 'API Deployment Checklist': Netlify (frontend), Modal (backend function), webhook integration with no-code platforms. Single page, actionable.
contradictions: Security stance: video discourages publishing AI-generated apps to public without security audit + custom domain (to avoid scanner/automated access), yet simultaneously shows ease of deploying to public URLs. Tension: build-fast culture vs. production-hardness.

Token cost philosophy: early content emphasizes 'cost is unavoidable, plan spend' (agent teams example: $80 for 15 min research), but later optimization section emphasizes 'minimize spend via compression'. No reconciliation of when to spend vs. when to optimize.

Agent autonomy: agent teams shown as powerful (parallel research, debate, merge) but also risky ('nuclear weapon aimed at your wallet'). Mitigation strategies aren't detailed (e.g., cost caps, per-agent token limits).

Modal pricing claim: '7x more expensive than Netlify' but also '$5 credits cover months of light usage' and '$0.30 per 1M tokens ultra cheap'. These statements don't reconcile cleanly; unclear if Modal is cheap or if Netlify is just free-tier.

Reusability claim: Skills presented as high-ROI for repetition, but video shows manual steps after skill creation (e.g., form filling, result review). Skill doesn't fully automate; human still in loop.
Context management tier 1 vs. optional: some techniques (like /compact) are presented as must-do early, then later presented as optional advanced technique. Prioritization unclear.
weird_gold: Adversarial agent debate pattern: spawn 2 agents (devil 1: 'findings not real', devil 2: 'findings real + need fixing'), have them argue back-and-forth to consensus. Directly borrowed from generative adversarial networks (ML concept). Higher quality than single-agent review.

Compaction as information density increase: Claude's auto-compact doesn't just shrink conversation; it increases token-per-information ratio. 'Netlify Rebuilds' becomes 'Netlify Rebuilding' = same info, fewer tokens. Enables more information in same token window. Counter-intuitive: compression improves output quality.
Fast mode multiplier: Opus 4.6 fast mode = 2.5x faster execution, 3x cost. Useful for time-critical work (lead scrape, morning briefing). Trade speed for cost explicitly quantified.

Sub-agent cost optimization: use cheaper models (Sonnet) for heavy computational work, Opus for orchestration. Saves tokens on repetitive tasks (code fixes, data entry, categorization) where intelligence is less critical than throughput.

Worktree isolation pattern: multiple agents on same repo but different branches prevents file conflicts without explicit coordination. Git's own conflict management is the coordination layer. Surprisingly elegant for parallel agent work.

Skills vs. Scripts distinction: skill = instruction file (MD checklist + optional code), script = inline code. Skills load on-demand, scripts don't. Allows for heavy-lifting code (web scraping, API calls) without constant token consumption.

Project memory compounding: first session = generic output, second session = output refined by first session's adjustments, Nth session = highly customized. Project memory is a state machine where each iteration improves.

Dispatch (SMS remote control): text Claude from phone, task runs on desktop, push notification when done. Phone is UI; desktop is compute. Inverts typical mobile app paradigm (usually mobile is primary).

Birthday API example: trivial use case (check if today is birthday) deployed to teach core pattern. Trivial endpoints are gateways to complex ones (webhook integrations, data processing, business logic).
gates: Security gate (before public deployment): have a developer do at least 1 security review pass. Cost: 'a few hundred dollars'. Liability risk without it: exposing user passwords, payment data, emails.

Token spend gate (before agent teams): estimate spend, ensure budget can absorb it. Example: $80 for 15-min security audit is good ROI if saving weeks of developer time. Example: $1.3M tokens for uncertain benefit is wasteful.
Skill evaluation gate (before production use): manually test output quality. Skill doesn't guarantee accuracy; human review needed to confirm before automation.
Context monitoring gate (before context rot): run /context every 2-3 sessions. Audit system tools vs. MCP overhead. If MCP is >10% of context, reduce server count.
Project setup gate (before recurring workflows): only create project for tasks you'll do 2+ times. Single-use tasks = chat or co-work session, not project.
Scheduled task test gate (before scheduling): run the prompt manually, review output, tweak until perfect. Only then schedule it. Prevents broken automations from running repeatedly.
Merge conflict gate (before agent team merges): have orchestration agent review all merge diffs before committing to main. Prevents silent data corruption.
